name: Sulfur hair darkening

lead: Sulphur hair restorers were popular from the 19th century as gradual-darkening tonics: users applied them daily and grey hair reportedly shaded back toward its earlier colour over days or weeks. The appeal was a natural-looking, younger appearance without a sudden dye job.

Analyses of well-known brands show the colour change came largely from lead acetate reacting with sulphur to form dark lead-sulphur compounds in the hair shaft. A 1912 British Medical Association analysis of Lockyer's Sulphur Hair Restorer listed lead acetate alongside sulphur and glycerine.

paras: Historically the tonic was a liquid applied to the hair and scalp repeatedly, with the shade deepening gradually. Modern progressive-darkening products work on similar principles, with some manufacturers using bismuth in place of lead.

Lead acetate is an accumulative poison, and 19th-century medical journals reported paralysis and at least one death linked to lead-based hair washes. Lead is banned in cosmetics in the EU, though lead-based darkeners can still be found elsewhere.

chain: Lead and sulphur compounds deposit in the hair shaft
angle.text: These tonics darkened grey hair progressively, letting users regain an earlier hair colour without a single dyeing session. Products used today that work the same way have replaced lead with other metals in some markets.

lead: Sulphur hair darkening refers to the 19th- and early 20th-century hair restorers, such as Lockyer's Sulphur Hair Restorer and Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, that gradually returned grey hair to a darker shade.[1][2] They were marketed as safe, quick and natural, and a rival to ordinary dyes.[2]

Analyses showed that these tonics typically contained both sulphur and lead acetate. A 1870 analysis reported sulphur, lead acetate and glycerine as the common ingredients, and the British Medical Association found lead acetate, lead sulphate and precipitated sulphur in Lockyer's in 1912.[1][2] The darkening is thought to come from sulphur compounds of lead depositing within the hair shaft.[3]
Medical commentators of the period warned that lead acetate is accumulative and had caused paralysis, and lead is now banned in EU cosmetics.[1][3]

paras: Progressive or gradual hair darkeners were sold as hair restorers. The classic formulas combined precipitated sulphur, lead acetate and glycerine in a scented water base such as rose water.[2] Modern commentary says these products work by depositing sulphur compounds of lead in the hair shaft, and that similar effects were sought in antiquity, when lead combs dipped in vinegar may have been used.[3]

An 1875 newspaper advertisement for Lockyer's described a bottle priced at 1s 6d that restored grey hair to its former colour within a few days and was harmless.[2] An 1870 report by surgeon Henry Matthews analysing widely advertised restorers found sulphur, lead acetate and glycerine, and an 1869 article called lead acetate an accumulative poison that had caused incurable paralysis.[1] The 1912 BMA analysis of Lockyer's gave proportions of about 1.6 parts lead acetate, 1.3 parts sulphur and 0.4 parts lead sulphate, and estimated the ingredients cost about tuppence against the retail price.[2]
An 1871 article suggested trying sulphur in water before lead dyes, saying it sometimes darkened grey hair within days.[1]

An 1870 committee report linked a death to use of a lead-based hair wash, and period journals warned of poisoning.[1] Lead acetate is described as toxic and as a reproductive toxicant in a 1997 review cited by Wikipedia.[4] Lead is banned in EU cosmetics; lead-based darkeners remain available in some markets outside the EU, mostly sold to men, while some manufacturers have substituted bismuth.[3]
No studies found. Two registered trials of N-acetylcysteine in trichotillomania concern hair pulling rather than hair colour.[5]
